QF.id: SIA Case Studies on SAS Standards_6

question.text: Pragati Foundation runs an education-support programme. The SIA observes that the SE's baseline data is missing for 3 of 12 indicators. Under SAS-100 materiality rules, the SIA should:

answer.text: Refuse to sign the Annual Impact Report until the SE re-collects baseline data retrospectively
Exclude those three indicators from the Report without comment
Replace the missing baseline with the national average for that indicator and proceed as if baseline were fully available

Assess materiality — if the missing indicators are quantitatively or qualitatively material, disclose the gap in Section III Limitations and consider a qualified conclusion; if immaterial, disclose and proceed

explanation.text: The Logic: SAS-100 follows the standard materiality and modified-conclusion architecture: (i) assess quantitative + qualitative materiality of the gap, (ii) disclose in Section III Limitations, (iii) modify the conclusion if the gap is material and pervasive. Retrospective baseline construction is often impossible, so honest disclosure is the defensible path. The Trap: Option A is disproportionate and impractical. Option B is concealment. Option C (use national averages) fabricates a counterfactual and violates the evidence standard. Cross-Exam Context: Mirrors the qualified-opinion / disclaimer logic in statutory audit treated in III-A (Compliance) and the research-report-limitation sections in XV (Research Analyst). Assessor's Pro-Tip: Write the Limitations paragraph with a two-column table: (a) indicator with missing baseline (b) assessed materiality (High/Med/Low) with a one-line rationale. This pre-empts peer-review questioning.
